assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: power
items.clue: The rate at which energy is transferred.

items.label: work done (W)
items.clue: What a force does when it moves an object, measured in joules.

items.label: Dissipation
items.clue: The spreading out of energy into stores that are less useful, most often the thermal store of the surroundings.

questions.stem: A hot metal block of mass m cools from 90 °C to 30 °C in still air. What does ∆E = m c ∆θ tell you about the block?

options.text: Nothing at all, because the equation applies only while a system is being heated up.
Its temperature has fallen, but the energy stored in the block has not changed at all.
The block's thermal energy store has fallen by m × c × 60, and that energy is released.
The block is now storing a total thermal energy of exactly m × c × 30 joules.

questions.stem: Two electric motors lift identical loads through the same height. Motor A takes 4 s and motor B takes 10 s. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Motor A is more powerful, because it must have done extra work on the load
Motor B is more powerful, because it keeps working for a longer time
Both motors have equal power, because the work done on the load is equal
Motor A is more powerful, because it does the same work in a shorter time

questions.explanation: Equal loads through equal heights means equal work done, so the shorter time gives the greater power.

questions.stem: In required practical activity 2, identical beakers of hot water are wrapped in different materials and the water temperature is recorded for ten minutes. Which result identifies the best insulator?

options.text: The beaker whose water fell in temperature by the smallest amount.
The beaker whose water fell in temperature by the largest amount of all.
The beaker whose water was the hottest when the timing started.
The beaker whose water ended at the temperature of the room.

questions.explanation: The best insulator gives the lowest rate of energy transfer, so its water stays hottest and drops least.

questions.stem: Water has a specific heat capacity of 4200 J/kg °C and aluminium has 900 J/kg °C. What does this tell you?

options.text: Water heats up faster than aluminium does when both are supplied with the same energy.
Warming 1 kg of water by 1 °C needs more energy than warming 1 kg of aluminium.
A kilogram of water always contains more thermal energy than a kilogram of aluminium.
The temperature rise of a substance is not related to the energy supplied to it.

questions.stem: A 1500 W heater is switched on for 300 s. How much energy does it transfer?

options.text: 5 J

questions.explanation: Rearranging P = E/t gives E = Pt = 1500 x 300 = 450 000 J.

questions.stem: A student investigates how the thickness of an insulating layer affects the cooling of hot water in a beaker. Which measurements should be taken?

options.text: The temperature of the water at the end of the run, and nothing else.
The temperature of the room, measured at the start and again at the end.
The thickness of the layer, and the water temperature at set times.
The mass of the insulation and the volume of the water used.

questions.explanation: AT 1 and AT 5 are exercised here: the length is measured with a ruler and the temperature is recorded against time.

questions.stem: In Required practical activity 1, how is the specific heat capacity of the metal block calculated?

options.text: By dividing the energy supplied by the mass and by the temperature rise.
By dividing the energy supplied by the temperature rise of the block only.
By dividing the energy supplied by the mass and by the starting temperature of the block.
By multiplying the energy supplied by the mass and by the temperature rise.

questions.explanation: c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ), which links the decrease of one energy store to the rise in temperature of the block.

questions.stem: The specification gives the equation P = W/t. What does W stand for in this equation?

options.text: the power in watts, as W is its unit
the work done, measured in newtons
the weight lifted, in newtons
the work done, measured in joules

questions.explanation: The specification pairs work done, W, with joules, J; power is the work done divided by the time.

questions.stem: The student repeats the cooling run three times for each material and calculates a mean temperature drop. Why is this done?

options.text: So that the water is given more time in which to cool down properly.
To reduce the effect of random error and give a more reliable result.
To make every material finish at the same final temperature.
So that the results appear more careful than one run would.

questions.explanation: Repeat readings scatter because of random variation; a mean of several runs is more reliable and reveals anomalies.

questions.stem: Which set of measurements is needed to determine the specific heat capacity of the block in this practical?

options.text: The mass of the block, the energy supplied by the heater, and the final temperature.
The mass of the block, the energy supplied by the heater, and the temperature rise.
The mass of the block, the power of the heater, and the temperature rise.
The energy supplied by the heater and the temperature rise of the block.

questions.explanation: These three quantities are exactly what c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ) needs, measured using AT 1 and AT 5 skills.

questions.stem: A motor transfers 15 000 J of energy in 2 minutes. What is its power?
questions.explanation: 2 minutes is 120 s, so P = E/t = 15 000 / 120 = 125 W.

questions.stem: Two identical 1 kg blocks of the same metal are heated. Block X rises by 10 °C and block Y rises by 30 °C. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Block Y has three times the specific heat capacity of X, because it became three times hotter.
Both blocks needed the same energy, because they have the same mass and are the same metal.
Block Y needed three times as much energy as X, because ∆E is proportional to ∆θ.
Block Y now stores three times as much thermal energy in total as block X does.
